nodes.name: NLS with inverse-square potential
nodes.statement: i\partial_t u + \Delta u + \frac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u &= 0, \quad u(0,\cdot)=u_0\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N),
nodes.statement_short: Focusing NLS with attractive inverse-square potential $c|x|^{-2}$ and $H^1$ initial data.
nodes.label: inls

nodes.name: Hardy constant $c_*$
nodes.statement: We shall fix the coupling constant $c\in(0,c_*)$, where $c_*=(N-2)^2/4$ is the best constant in Hardy's inequality:

nodes.name: Hardy's inequality
nodes.statement: c_*\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}dx \le \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\nabla u|^2 dx, \quad u\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N).
conclusions: c_*\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}dx \le \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\nabla u|^2 dx
nodes.label: hardy

nodes.name: Mass conservation
nodes.statement: \Vert u(t)\Vert_{L^2_x} \equiv \Vert u_0\Vert_{L^2_x},
nodes.statement_short: Conservation of the $L^2$ norm (mass) along the flow.
nodes.label: mass

nodes.name: Energy conservation
nodes.statement: E(u(t))=\frac12 \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u(t,x)|^2\,\mathrm{d} x - \frac{c}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{|u(t,x)|^2}{|x|^2}dx - \frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u(t,x)|^{p+1}\,\mathrm{d} x \equiv E(u_0).
nodes.statement_short: Definition and conservation of the energy $E$.
nodes.label: energy

nodes.name: global solution
nodes.statement: A solution is called global if $T=+\infty$.

nodes.name: Local well-posedness and blow-up alternative
nodes.statement: Let $c\in(0,c_*)$ and $1<p<1+\frac{4}{N-2}$. For any initial value $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, there exists $T\in(0,+\infty]$ and a maximal solution $u\in C^0_t H^1_x ([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^N)$ of \eqref{inls}, satisfying \eqref{mass}--\eqref{energy} for all $t\in(0,T)$. Moreover, the blow-up alternative holds: if $T<+\infty$ then $\lim_{t\uparrow T} \Vert \nabla u(t)\Vert_{L^2}=+\infty$. Finally, if $1<p<1+\frac{4}{N}$, then the solution is global.
conclusions: there exists $T\in(0,+\infty]$ and a maximal solution $u\in C^0_t H^1_x ([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^N)$ of \eqref{inls}, satisfying \eqref{mass}--\eqref{energy} for all $t\in(0,T)$.
if $T<+\infty$ then $\lim_{t\uparrow T} \Vert \nabla u(t)\Vert_{L^2}=+\infty$.
if $1<p<1+\frac{4}{N}$, then the solution is global.
nodes.statement_short: Local well-posedness in $H^1$ with conservation laws and the blow-up alternative; global existence for mass-subcritical $p$.
nodes.label: local.thm

nodes.name: Symmetries of NLS with inverse-square potential
nodes.statement: More precisely, if $u(t,x)$ solves~\eqref{inls}, then so do: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)] \item $u_{t_0}(t,x)=u(t-t_0,x)$, for all $t_0\in\mathbb{R}$ (time translation invariance); \item $u_{\gamma_0}(t,x)=e^{i\gamma_0}u(t,x)$, for all $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ (phase invariance); \item $u_{\lambda_0}(t,x)=\lambda_0^{2/(p-1)}u(\lambda_0^2t,\lambda_0x)$, for all $\lambda_0>0$ (scaling invariance). \end{enumerate}
conclusions: $u_{t_0}(t,x)=u(t-t_0,x)$, for all $t_0\in\mathbb{R}$ (time translation invariance);
$u_{\gamma_0}(t,x)=e^{i\gamma_0}u(t,x)$, for all $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ (phase invariance);
$u_{\lambda_0}(t,x)=\lambda_0^{2/(p-1)}u(\lambda_0^2t,\lambda_0x)$, for all $\lambda_0>0$ (scaling invariance).
nodes.statement_short: Solutions are invariant under time translation, phase rotation and scaling.

nodes.name: Hardy functional
nodes.statement: For our analysis it is convenient to introduce the {\em Hardy functional}, defined on $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ by \[ H(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\nabla u|^2dx -c\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}dx. \]

nodes.name: Hardy-functional equivalence bounds
nodes.statement: \left(1-\frac{c}{c_*}\right) \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\nabla u|^2dx\le H(u)\le \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\nabla u|^2dx.
nodes.statement_short: $H(u)$ is bounded above by $\|\nabla u\|_2^2$ and below by $(1-c/c_*)\|\nabla u\|_2^2$.
nodes.label: hardy2

nodes.name: Equivalence of $H$ and the $\dot H^1$ seminorm
nodes.statement: In particular, for $c\in(0,c_*)$, $H(u)$ defines on $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ a seminorm equivalent to $\Vert\nabla u\Vert_{L^2}$.
conclusions: $H(u)$ defines on $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ a seminorm equivalent to $\Vert\nabla u\Vert_{L^2}$

nodes.name: Blow-up criterion in terms of $H$
nodes.statement: A solution $u(t)$ therefore blows up at time $T>0$ if and only if $\lim_{t\uparrow T} H(u(t))=+\infty$.
conclusions: blows up at time $T>0$ if and only if $\lim_{t\uparrow T} H(u(t))=+\infty$

nodes.name: $L^2$ scaling
nodes.statement: Now, $p=1+\frac{4}{N}$ yields $2/(p-1)=N/2$ and, as in the classical case $c=0$, \eqref{inls} is invariant under the {\em $L^2$ scaling} \[ u(t,x) \to u_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda^{N/2}u(\lambda^2 t, \lambda x) \quad (\lambda>0). \]
nodes.statement_short: For $p=1+4/N$, the equation is invariant under $u\mapsto\lambda^{N/2}u(\lambda^2t,\lambda x)$.

nodes.name: $L^2$ critical
nodes.statement: This transformation preserves the $L^2$ norm and \eqref{inls} is called {\em $L^2$ critical}.

nodes.name: Standing waves and the stationary equation
nodes.statement: Indeed, $u(t,x)=e^{it}\varphi(x)$ is a (global) solution of~\eqref{inls} if and only if $\varphi\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ solves the nonlinear elliptic equation \begin{equation} \Delta\varphi + \frac{c}{|x|^2}\varphi - \varphi + |\varphi|^{\frac{4}{N}}\varphi=0. \end{equation}
conclusions: $u(t,x)=e^{it}\varphi(x)$ is a (global) solution of~\eqref{inls} if and only if
nodes.statement_short: $e^{it}\varphi$ solves the NLS iff $\varphi$ solves the stationary elliptic equation.

nodes.name: Stationary equation for standing waves
nodes.statement: \Delta\varphi + \frac{c}{|x|^2}\varphi - \varphi + |\varphi|^{\frac{4}{N}}\varphi=0.
nodes.label: sinls

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the ground state for $c=0$
nodes.statement: For $c=0$, it is well known that the ground state is unique, up to the symmetries of \eqref{sinls}. More precisely, there exists a unique positive radial solution $Q\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ of \eqref{sinls}, and $\mathcal{G}=\{e^{i\gamma_0}Q(\cdot - x_0) : \gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}, \ x_0\in\mathbb{R}^N\}$.
conclusions: there exists a unique positive radial solution $Q\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ of \eqref{sinls}

nodes.name: Uniqueness of ground states for $c>0$
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, for $c>0$, we are not aware of any uniqueness result for \eqref{sinls} on $\mathbb{R}^N$.

nodes.name: Sharp global well-posedness below the ground-state mass
nodes.statement: Let $c\in(0,c_*)$ and $p=1+\frac{4}{N}$. If $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ satisfies \begin{equation} \Vert u_0\Vert_{L^2}<M_\mathrm{gs}, \end {equation} then the corresponding solution of \eqref{inls} given by Theorem~\ref{local.thm} is global.
conclusions: then the corresponding solution of \eqref{inls} given by Theorem~\ref{local.thm} is global.
nodes.statement_short: Solutions with mass strictly below the ground-state mass $M_{gs}$ are global.
nodes.label: global.thm

nodes.name: Subcritical mass condition
nodes.statement: \Vert u_0\Vert_{L^2}<M_\mathrm{gs},
nodes.label: sharp

nodes.name: Energy lower bound in terms of mass
nodes.statement: E(u)\ge \frac12 H(u) \left(1-\left(\frac{\Vert u\Vert_{L^2}}{M_\mathrm{gs}}\right)^\frac{4}{N}\right), \quad u\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N),
nodes.label: posE

nodes.name: A priori bound on $H(u(t))$
nodes.statement: H(u(t)) \le 2E(u_0) \left(1-\left(\frac{\Vert u\Vert_{L^2}}{M_\mathrm{gs}}\right)^\frac{4}{N}\right)^{-1},
nodes.label: subcritical

nodes.name: Explicit minimal mass blow-up solutions $S_{Q,T,\lambda_0,\gamma_0}$
nodes.statement: S_{Q,T,\lambda_0,\gamma_0}(t,x) = e^{i\gamma_0} e^{i\frac{\lambda_0^2}{T-t}} e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}} \left(\frac{\lambda_0}{T-t}\right)^{N/2}Q\left( \frac{\lambda_0x}{T-t} \right).
nodes.statement_short: Pseudo-conformal transform of the rescaled, phase-shifted standing wave $e^{it}Q$.
nodes.label: S1.def

nodes.name: Classification of minimal mass blow-up solutions
nodes.statement: Let $T>0$ and $u\in C\big([0,T),H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)\big)$ be a minimal mass solution of~\eqref{inls} with $p=1+\frac{4}{N}$, which blows up at time $T$, \emph{i.e.}~$\Vert u_0\Vert_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $\lim_{t\uparrow T} H(u(t))=+\infty$. Then there exist a ground state $Q\in \mathcal{G}$, $\lambda_0>0$ and $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ such that, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ u(t)=S_{Q,T,\lambda_0,\gamma_0}(t). \]
assumptions: Let $T>0$ and $u\in C\big([0,T),H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)\big)$ be a minimal mass solution of~\eqref{inls} with $p=1+\frac{4}{N}$, which blows up at time $T$,
conclusions: Then there exist a ground state $Q\in \mathcal{G}$, $\lambda_0>0$ and $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ such that, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ u(t)=S_{Q,T,\lambda_0,\gamma_0}(t). \]
nodes.statement_short: Every minimal mass blow-up solution is, up to symmetries, the pseudo-conformal transform of a ground state.
nodes.label: main.thm

nodes.name: Local well-posedness at the threshold $c=c_*$
nodes.statement: However, it is not clear to us that local well-posedness holds in this case.

nodes.name: Breakdown of the compactness argument at $c=c_*$
nodes.statement: Note that, for $c=c_*$, inequality \eqref{crucial} also breaks down, and we do not know how to prove the crucial Proposition~\ref{compact.prop}.

nodes.name: Weinstein functional
nodes.statement: Consider the Weinstein functional \[ J^{p,N}(u):=\frac{H(u)^{\frac{p-1}{4}N}\|u\|^{2+\frac{p-1}{2}(2-N)}_{L^2}}{\|u\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}}. \]
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Existence of minimizers of the Weinstein functional
nodes.statement: For $1<p<1+\frac{4}{N-2}$, \[ \alpha_{p,N} := \inf_{u\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)\backslash\{0\}} J^{p,N}(u) \] is attained at a positive radial function $Q\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, solution of the Euler--Lagrange equation \begin{equation} N\Big(\frac{p-1}{4}\Big)\Big(\Delta Q +c\frac{Q}{|x|^2}\Big)-\left(1+\frac{p-1}{4}(2-N)\right)Q+Q^p=0. \end{equation} Furthermore, \begin{equation} \alpha_{p,N}=2\frac{\|Q\|_{L^2}^{p-1}}{p+1}. \end{equation} In the case $p=1+\frac4N$, any minimizer of $J^{p,N}$ can be rescaled into a solution of \eqref{sinls}.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion
conclusions: is attained at a positive radial function $Q\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, solution of the Euler--Lagrange equation
In the case $p=1+\frac4N$, any minimizer of $J^{p,N}$ can be rescaled into a solution of \eqref{sinls}.
nodes.statement_short: The infimum $\alpha_{p,N}$ of the Weinstein functional is attained at a positive radial solution $Q$ of the Euler-Lagrange equation.
nodes.label: minimization.prop

nodes.name: Euler--Lagrange equation for the minimizer
nodes.statement: N\Big(\frac{p-1}{4}\Big)\Big(\Delta Q +c\frac{Q}{|x|^2}\Big)-\left(1+\frac{p-1}{4}(2-N)\right)Q+Q^p=0.

nodes.label: EL

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: First note that the functional $J^{p,N}$ is invariant under the scaling \[ u(x) \to u^{\lambda,\mu}(x):=\mu u(\lambda x) \quad (\lambda,\mu>0). \] Indeed, we have \begin{align*} H (u^{\lambda,\mu})&=\lambda^{2-N}\mu^2 H (u),\\ \|u^{\lambda,\mu}\|_{L^2}^2&=\lambda^{-N}\mu^2\|u\|^2_{L^2},\\ \|u^{\lambda,\mu}\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}&=\lambda^{-N}\mu^{p+1}\|u\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}\\ \text{and so} \quad J^{p,N}(u^{\lambda,\mu})&=J^{p,N}(u). \end{align*} Let $\{u_n\}\subset H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ be a minimizing sequence, $\alpha_{p,N} = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} J^{p,N}(u_n)\ge0$. Since $J(|u|)\le J(u)$, we can suppose that $u_n\ge0$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Furthermore, denoting by $u_n^*$ the Schwarz symmetrization of $u_n$ (see e.g.~\cite[pp.~80-83]{Lieb}), we have that \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{(u_n^*)^{2}}{|x|^2} dx \ge \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{u_n^{2}}{|x|^2} dx, \] \[ \Vert \nabla u_n^*\Vert_{L^2}\le \Vert \nabla u_n\Vert_{L^2} \quad\text{and}\quad \Vert u_n^*\Vert_{L^2}\le\Vert u_n\Vert_{L^2}. \] We can therefore suppose that $u_n=u_n^*$ and, in particular, that each $u_n$ is positive, radial and radially decreasing. Thanks to the scaling invariance of $J^{p,N}$, we can further rescale the minimizing sequence by choosing $\lambda_n=\|u_n\|_{L^2}/H(u_n) $ and $\mu_n=\|u_n\|_{L^2}^{N/2-1}/H^{N/2}(u_n)$. We thus obtain a minimizing sequence $\psi_n=u_n^{\lambda_n,\mu_n}$ with the following properties: \begin{align*} \psi_n \ge 0, \quad \psi_n=\psi_n(|x|),\\ \|\psi_n\|_{L^2}=1, \quad H(\psi_n)=1,\\ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} J^{p,N}(\psi_n)=\alpha_{p,N}. \end{align*} In particular, $\{\psi_n\}$ is bounded in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Thus, up to a subsequence, we can suppose that $\{\psi_n\}$ has a weak limit $\psi^* \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Since $\{\psi_n\}\subset H^1_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, we can also suppose that $\psi_n$ converges strongly to $\psi^*$ in $L^{p+1}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. By weak lower semi-continuity of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_{L^2}$ and $H$ (see \cite{montefusco}), we obtain that $\|\psi^*\|_{L^2}\le 1$ and $H(\psi^*)\le 1$. Hence, \[ \alpha_{p,N}\le J^{p,N}(\psi^*)\le \frac{1}{\|\psi^*\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}J^{p,N}(\psi_n)=\alpha_{p,N}. \] It follows that $H(\psi^*)^{\frac{p-1}{4}N}\|\psi^*\|_{L^2}^{2+(p-1)(2-N)/2}=1$ and, therefore, $H(\psi^*)=\|\psi^*\|_{L^2}=1$. Now, $\psi^*$ must satisfy the Euler--Lagrange equation $DJ^{p,N}(\psi^*)=0$. We first remark that, for any $u \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, $DJ^{p,N}(u)=0$ reads \begin{equation} -N\Big(\frac{p-1}{4}\Big)\Big(\Delta u + \frac{c}{|x|^2} u\Big) +\Big(1+ \frac{p-1}{4}(2-N)\Big)\frac{H(u)}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2} u -\Big(\frac{p+1}{2}\Big) \frac{H(u)}{\|u\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}}|u|^{p-1}u=0. \end{equation} Taking into consideration $H(\psi^*)=1$, $\| \psi^*\|_{L^2}=1$, $\|\psi^*\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}=\alpha_{p,N}^{-1}$ and $\psi^*\ge0$, we get \[ N\Big(\frac{p-1}{4}\Big)\Big(\Delta \psi^*+c\frac{\psi^*}{|x|^2}\Big) -\left(1+\frac{p-1}{4}(2-N) \right)\psi^*+\alpha_{p,N}\Big(\frac{p+1}{2}\Big)(\psi^*)^p=0. \] Then $Q$ defined by $\psi^*=(\alpha_{p,N}(p+1)/2)^{-1/(p-1)}Q$ readily satisfies (\ref{EL}) and \eqref{sharpestimate}. Finally, in view of Remark~\ref{gs_scaling.rem} and Remark~\ref{scaling.rem} below, if $p=1+\frac4N$ and $u$ is a minimizer of $J^{1+\frac{4}{N},N}$, the Euler--Lagrange equation \eqref{euler} reads \begin{equation} \Delta u + \frac{c}{|x|^2} u -\frac{2}{N}\frac{H(u)}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2} u +|u|^{p-1}u=0, \end{equation} and any solution $u$ can be rescaled into a solution $Q$ of \eqref{sinls} by letting \[ u(x)=\lambda^{N/2}Q(\lambda x) \quad\text{with}\quad \lambda=\sqrt{\frac{2}{N}}\frac{\sqrt{H(u)}}{\Vert u\Vert_{L^2}}. \] The proof is complete.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: ~{\it Theorem~\ref{global.thm}}. Consider a local solution of \eqref{inls}, as given by Theorem~\ref{local.thm}. By the blow-up alternative, we need only show that, if $\Vert u_0\Vert_{L^2}<M_\text{gs}$, then $H(u(t))$ remains bounded. We control $H(u(t))$ using the energy. By definition of $E$, \[ H(u)=2E(u) + \frac{1}{1+\frac2N}\Vert{u}\Vert_{L^{2+\frac4N}}^{2+\frac4N}. \] Now, by Corollary~\ref{GN.cor}, \[ \|u\|_{L^{2+\frac4N}}^{2+\frac4N}\le \left(\frac{1+\frac2N}{M_\text{gs}^{\frac4N}}\right) H(u)\|u\|_{L^2}^{\frac4N} =(1+\textstyle\frac2N)\displaystyle\left(\frac{\|u\|_{L^2}}{M_\text{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(u). \] Hence, by conservation of mass and energy, \begin{align*} H(u(t)) &\le 2E(u(t))+\left(\frac{\|u(t)\|_{L^2}}{M_\text{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(u(t))\\ &\phantom{\le}=2E(u_0)+\left(\frac{\|u_0\|_{L^2}}{M_\text{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(u(t)). \end{align*} It follows that \[ \left(1-\left(\frac{\|u_0\|_{L^2}}{M_\text{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}\right)H(u(t))\le 2 E(u_0), \] which concludes the proof.

nodes.statement: Let $u$ be a global solution of \eqref{inls}. Then, for all $T\in\mathbb{R}$, the function \[ u_T(t,x)=\frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2}}u\left(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\right) \] is a solution of \eqref{inls} on $(-\infty, T)$, with $\|u_T\|_{L^2}=\|u\|_{L^2}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Straightforward calculations give \[ \partial_t u_T(t,x) = \frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}} \left[ \frac{N}{2}(T-t)u -i\frac{|x|^2}{4}u +\partial_t u +x\cdot\nabla u \right]\! \left(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\right) \] and \[ \Delta u_T(t,x) = \frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}} \left[ -\frac{|x|^2}{4}u -i\frac{N}{2}(T-t)u -ix\cdot\nabla u +\Delta u\right]\! \left(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\right) \] for the derivatives. For the nonlinear term we find \[ |u_T|^{\frac{4}{N}}u_T(t,x)= \frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}}|u|^{\frac{4}{N}}u\Big(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\Big), \] and for the potential term \[ c|x|^{-2}u_T(t,x)= c\Big|\frac{x}{T-t}\Big|^{-2}\frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}}u\Big(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\Big). \] It then follows from \eqref{inls} that \[ \begin{split} i\partial u_T(t,x)+&\Delta u_T(t,x)+c|x|^{-2}u_T(t,x)+|u_T|^{4/N}u_T(t,x) \\ &=\frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}}[i\partial_tu+\Delta u+c|x|^{-2}u +|u|^{4/N}u]\Big(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\Big)=0, \end{split} \] which proves the lemma.

nodes.name: Ground states have minimal mass among stationary solutions
nodes.statement: It follows from Lemma~\ref{pseudo-conf.lem} that any solution $\varphi$ of \eqref{sinls} satisfies $\|\varphi\|_{L^2}\ge M_\mathrm{gs}$. Otherwise, applying Lemma~\ref{pseudo-conf.lem} with $u(t,x)=e^{it}\varphi(x)$, one could construct a finite time blow-up solution below the minimal mass threshold, which would contradict our global well-posedness result, Theorem~\ref{global.thm}.

nodes.name: Reduction of the blow-up family to a single solution $S$
nodes.statement: Note that the blow-up solutions of the family exhibited in Proposition~\ref{blow-up_sol.prop} can all be retrieved from the solution \[ S(t,x) := S_{0,1,0}(t,x) = e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} e^{-\frac{i}{t}} \frac{1}{|t|^{N/2}}Q\left(-\frac{x}{t}\right), \] defined on $(-\infty,0)$ and which blows up at $t=0$ with speed \[ \Vert\nabla S(t)\Vert_{L^2} \sim \frac{C}{|t|}\quad \text{as } t\uparrow0, \] for some $C>0$. Indeed, all the solutions $S_{Q,T,\lambda_0,\gamma_0}$ are equal to $S$, up to the symmetries (a), (b) and (c) stated in the introduction. Namely, if we apply the changes $u(t,x)\to \lambda_0^{-N/2}u(\lambda_0^{-2}t,\lambda_0^{-1}x)$, $u(t,x)\to u(t-T,x)$ and finally $u(t,x)\to e^{i\gamma_0}u(t,x)$ to $S$, we obtain $S_{Q,T,\lambda_0,\gamma_0}$.

nodes.name: concentration-compactness lemma
nodes.statement:
Let $\{v_n\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\subset H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ satisfy \[ \lim_{n ightarrow\infty}\|v_n\|_{L^2}=M<+\infty \quad 	ext{and} \quad \sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} H(v_n) <+\infty. \] Then there exists a subsequence $\{v_{n_k}\}_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ that satisfies one of the following properties. \medskip 
oindent (V) $\|v_{n_k}\|_{L^q}ightarrow 0$ as $kightarrow\infty$ for all $q\in(2,2^*)$. \medskip 
oindent (D) There are sequences ${w_k},{z_k}\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and a constant $\alpha\in (0,1)$ such that:  egin{enumerate} \item $\dist(\supp(w_k),\supp(z_k))ightarrow\infty$; \item $|v_k|+|z_k|\le |v_{n_k}|$; \item $\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}} (\|w_k\|_{H^1}+\|z_k\|_{H^1})<+\infty$; \item $\|w_k\|_{L^2}ightarrow\alpha M$ and $\|z_k\|_{L^2}	o (1-\alpha)M$ as $kightarrow\infty$; \item $\lim_{kightarrow\infty} ig| \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|^q-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^q-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|z_k|^q ig|=0$ for all $q\in[2,2^*)$; \item $\liminf_{kightarrow\infty} ig\{ H(v_{n_k})-H(w_k)-H(z_k)  ig\}\ge 0$. \end{enumerate} \medskip 
oindent (C) There exists $v\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and a sequence $\{y_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset \mathbb{R}^N$ such that \[ v_{n_k}(\cdot -y_k)ightarrow v \quad 	ext{in} \quad L^q(\mathbb{R}^N), \quad  orall q\in[2,2^*). \]
conclusions: Then there exists a subsequence $\{v_{n_k}\}_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ that satisfies one of the following properties.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement:
The behavior of the sequence $\{v_n\}$ is constrained by the concentration-compactness lemma. Our proof proceeds in several steps: by ruling out (V) and (D), we will first show that property (C) holds in Lemma~ef{conc-comp.lemma}. We will then prove the localization of the subsequence $\{v_{n_k}\}$, {\em i.e.}~that the sequence of translations ${y_k}$ is bounded in $\mathbb{R}^N$. This step is the most delicate one due to the inverse-square potential, and will be handled by a subtle combination of Hardy's inequality and the Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality \eqref{GN}. Once this localization property is established, the result will follow from Proposition~ef{charact.prop}. \medskip 
oindent {\em Step~1: Compactness in $L^q(\mathbb{R}^N)$.} First suppose that (V) holds. Since $p+1\in (2,2^*)$ we get, \[ \limsup_{kightarrow\infty} E(v_{n_k})=\limsup_{kightarrow\infty}\Big\{ rac{1}{2}H(v_{n_k})- rac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx\Big\}= rac{1}{2}\limsup_{kightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})>0, \] which contradicts our assumptions. Suppose now that (D) holds. Then from properties (5) and (6) it follows that \[  egin{split} \limsup_{kightarrow\infty}\{E(w_k)+E(z_k)\}&\le rac{1}{2}\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}) - rac{1}{p+1}\limsup_{kightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|dx \ &\le\limsup_{kightarrow\infty} E(v_{n_k})\le 0. \end{split} \] Property (D)(4) of Lemma (ef{conc-comp.lemma}) and inequality \eqref{posE} imply that $E(w_k), E(z_k)\ge 0$ for $k$ large enough, thus \[ E(w_k)ightarrow 0 \quad 	ext{and} \quad E(z_k)ightarrow 0. \] Using again property (4) and inequality \eqref{posE}, we get that \[ H(w_k)ightarrow 0 \quad	ext{and}\quad H(z_k)ightarrow 0. \] Hence, \[ \lim_{kightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx =\lim_{kightarrow\infty}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|z_k|^{p+1}dxight)=0, \] leading again to the contradiction that $\limsup_{kightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})>0$. oindent {\em Step~2: Localization.} We now prove by contradiction that the sequence of translations $\{y_k\}$ is bounded in $\mathbb{R}^N$. We first observe that, by the boundedness of $\{v_{n_k}\}$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$, there exists $C\ge0$ such that \[ \mathrm{II}_k\le R^{-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}(x)|^2dx\le CR^{-2}. \] By choosing $R>0$ large, we can thus make $\mathrm{II}_k$ as small as we want, uniformly in $k$. Next, we fix $R>0$ arbitrary and prove that $\lim_{k	o\infty}\mathrm{I}_k=0$. This will complete the proof of \eqref{zerolimit}. We argue by contradiction and suppose there exist $\delta>0$ and a subsequence of $\{v_{n_k}\}$ (still denoted $\{v_{n_k}\}$) such that  egin{equation*} \liminf_{kightarrow\infty}\int_{|x|<R} rac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx\ge\delta. \end{equation*} Note that this inequality will still hold if we increase the value of $R$ or pass to a further subsequence. Then define \[ u_k(x)=\varphi(|x|) v_{n_k}(x) \quad	ext{and}\quad w_k(x)=(1-\varphi(|x|))v_{n_k}(x). \] We clearly have $|u_k|,|w_k|\le|v_{n_k}|$, and $\{u_k\},\{w_k\}\subset H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ with \[ |

To prove \eqref{est0}, we use the above properties of $u_k$ and $w_k$ to observe that  egin{multline} \left|\int_{R<|x|<R+a}\Big[|

We will now combine \eqref{e1} with the Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality \eqref{GN} and the assumption on the energy in \eqref{a} to reach a contradiction. Using Step 1 with $|y_k|	o\infty$, we have that $u_k	o0$ in $L^{p+1}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Hence, by \eqref{a},  egin{align*} \limsup_{kightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})\le rac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx = rac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx, \end{align*} and so, by \eqref{e1},  egin{align} \liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(w_k)< rac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx. \end{align} Using again Step 1 with $|y_k|	o\infty$, we also have that $u_k	o0$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$, which implies \[ M_\mathrm{gs}=\lim_{kightarrow\infty}\|v_{n_k}\|_{L^2} =\lim_{kightarrow\infty}\|w_k\|_{L^2}. \] Therefore, \eqref{GN} applied to $w_k$ yields \[  rac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx \le\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}\left( rac{\|w_k\|_{L^2}}{M_\mathrm{gs}}ight)^{ rac4N}H(w_k) = \liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(w_k), \] which, together with \eqref{e4}, leads to the contradiction \[ \liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(w_k)<\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(w_k). \] This shows that $\lim_{k	o\infty}\mathrm{I}_k=0$ and completes the proof of \eqref{zerolimit}. We now have  egin{align*} \liminf_{k	o\infty} E(v_{n_k}) &=\liminf_{k	o\infty}  rac12 \|
abla v_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 -\lim_{k	o\infty}  rac{1}{p+1} \| v_{n_k}\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\ &=\liminf_{k	o\infty}  rac12 \|
abla \widetilde{v}_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 -\lim_{k	o\infty}  rac{1}{p+1} \| \widetilde{v}_{n_k}\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\ &\ge  rac12 \|

oindent {\em Step~3: Conclusion.} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $y_k	o y^*\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Then \[ v_{n_k}	o v^*=v(\cdot+y^*) \quad 	ext{in} \quad L^q(\mathbb{R}^N), \quad  orall q\in[2,2^*), \] and $v_{n_k}ightharpoonup v^*$ weakly in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Since the Hardy functional $H$ is weakly lower semi-continuous \cite{montefusco}, and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, it now follows by \eqref{posE} that \[  egin{split} 0\le E(v^*)= rac{1}{2}H(v^*)- rac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx &\le  rac{1}{2}\limsup_{kightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})- rac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx\ &\phantom{\le}=\limsup_{kightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})\le 0, \end{split} \] so in fact  egin{equation} E(v^*)=0 \quad	ext{and}\quad H(v^*)=\lim_{kightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}). \end{equation} Since $\|v^*\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(v^*)=0$, Proposition ef{charact.prop} yields $v^*=e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda_0>0$, and some $Q\in \mathcal{G}$. Finally, by \eqref{convergence} and \eqref{hardy2}, we also have that $\|v_{n_k}\|_{H^1}ightarrow \|v^*\|_{H^1}$. Hence $\{v_{n_k}\}$ converges strongly to $v^*$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, which completes the proof.

nodes.name: Virial identity in the $L^2$ critical case
nodes.statement: In the $L^2$ critical case, $p=1+\frac{4}{N}$, (\ref{virialtwo}) reduces to \begin{equation} \Gamma''(t)=16E(u_0). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Banica's Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
nodes.statement_short: At ground-state mass, the momentum against $\nabla\theta$ is bounded by $\sqrt{2E(u)}$ times a weighted $L^2$ norm.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Rescale along $t_n\uparrow T$ and use compactness to get mass concentration at 0; then Banica's inequality and the virial identity force $\Gamma(t)=8E(u_0)(T-t)^2$. A phase modulation of $u_0$ then has zero energy, so Proposition 3 and uniqueness identify $u$ with $S_{Q,T,\lambda_0,\gamma_0}$.

nodes.name: Convergence of rescaled $v_n$
nodes.statement: \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \|v_n-e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}\|_{H^1}=0,

nodes.statement: \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0).

nodes.name: Scaling invariance of $J$
nodes.statement: First note that the functional $J^{p,N}$ is invariant under the scaling \[ u(x) \to u^{\lambda,\mu}(x):=\mu u(\lambda x) \quad (\lambda,\mu>0). \] Indeed, we have \begin{align*} H (u^{\lambda,\mu})&=\lambda^{2-N}\mu^2 H (u),\\ \|u^{\lambda,\mu}\|_{L^2}^2&=\lambda^{-N}\mu^2\|u\|^2_{L^2},\\ \|u^{\lambda,\mu}\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}&=\lambda^{-N}\mu^{p+1}\|u\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}\\ \text{and so} \quad J^{p,N}(u^{\lambda,\mu})&=J^{p,N}(u). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Show $J^{p,N}$ is invariant under $u\mapsto\mu u(\lambda x)$.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Minimizing sequence
nodes.statement: Let $\{u_n\}\subset H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ be a minimizing sequence, $\alpha_{p,N} = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} J^{p,N}(u_n)\ge0$. Since $J(|u|)\le J(u)$, we can suppose that $u_n\ge0$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a nonnegative minimizing sequence.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Schwarz symmetrization
nodes.statement: Furthermore, denoting by $u_n^*$ the Schwarz symmetrization of $u_n$ (see e.g.~\cite[pp.~80-83]{Lieb}), we have that \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{(u_n^*)^{2}}{|x|^2} dx \ge \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{u_n^{2}}{|x|^2} dx, \] \[ \Vert \nabla u_n^*\Vert_{L^2}\le \Vert \nabla u_n\Vert_{L^2} \quad\text{and}\quad \Vert u_n^*\Vert_{L^2}\le\Vert u_n\Vert_{L^2}. \] We can therefore suppose that $u_n=u_n^*$ and, in particular, that each $u_n$ is positive, radial and radially decreasing.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $u_n$ by its Schwarz symmetrization, which does not increase $J$.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Normalized sequence
nodes.statement: Thanks to the scaling invariance of $J^{p,N}$, we can further rescale the minimizing sequence by choosing $\lambda_n=\|u_n\|_{L^2}/H(u_n) $ and $\mu_n=\|u_n\|_{L^2}^{N/2-1}/H^{N/2}(u_n)$. We thus obtain a minimizing sequence $\psi_n=u_n^{\lambda_n,\mu_n}$ with the following properties: \begin{align*} \psi_n \ge 0, \quad \psi_n=\psi_n(|x|),\\ \|\psi_n\|_{L^2}=1, \quad H(\psi_n)=1,\\ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} J^{p,N}(\psi_n)=\alpha_{p,N}. \end{align*} In particular, $\{\psi_n\}$ is bounded in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale to $\|\psi_n\|_2=H(\psi_n)=1$; bounded in $H^1$.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Weak limit is a minimizer
nodes.statement: Thus, up to a subsequence, we can suppose that $\{\psi_n\}$ has a weak limit $\psi^* \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Since $\{\psi_n\}\subset H^1_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, we can also suppose that $\psi_n$ converges strongly to $\psi^*$ in $L^{p+1}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. By weak lower semi-continuity of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_{L^2}$ and $H$ (see \cite{montefusco}), we obtain that $\|\psi^*\|_{L^2}\le 1$ and $H(\psi^*)\le 1$. Hence, \[ \alpha_{p,N}\le J^{p,N}(\psi^*)\le \frac{1}{\|\psi^*\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}J^{p,N}(\psi_n)=\alpha_{p,N}. \] It follows that $H(\psi^*)^{\frac{p-1}{4}N}\|\psi^*\|_{L^2}^{2+(p-1)(2-N)/2}=1$ and, therefore, $H(\psi^*)=\|\psi^*\|_{L^2}=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Radial compactness and weak lsc give a minimizer $\psi^*$ with $H=\|\cdot\|_2=1$.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Euler--Lagrange equation
nodes.statement: Now, $\psi^*$ must satisfy the Euler--Lagrange equation $DJ^{p,N}(\psi^*)=0$. We first remark that, for any $u \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, $DJ^{p,N}(u)=0$ reads \begin{equation} -N\Big(\frac{p-1}{4}\Big)\Big(\Delta u + \frac{c}{|x|^2} u\Big) +\Big(1+ \frac{p-1}{4}(2-N)\Big)\frac{H(u)}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2} u -\Big(\frac{p+1}{2}\Big) \frac{H(u)}{\|u\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}}|u|^{p-1}u=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write the Euler-Lagrange equation $DJ^{p,N}=0$.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Rescale to $Q$
nodes.statement: Taking into consideration $H(\psi^*)=1$, $\| \psi^*\|_{L^2}=1$, $\|\psi^*\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}}=\alpha_{p,N}^{-1}$ and $\psi^*\ge0$, we get \[ N\Big(\frac{p-1}{4}\Big)\Big(\Delta \psi^*+c\frac{\psi^*}{|x|^2}\Big) -\left(1+\frac{p-1}{4}(2-N) \right)\psi^*+\alpha_{p,N}\Big(\frac{p+1}{2}\Big)(\psi^*)^p=0. \] Then $Q$ defined by $\psi^*=(\alpha_{p,N}(p+1)/2)^{-1/(p-1)}Q$ readily satisfies (\ref{EL}) and \eqref{sharpestimate}.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaling $\psi^*$ gives $Q$ solving (EL) with the value of $\alpha_{p,N}$.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Critical case rescaling
nodes.statement: Finally, in view of Remark~\ref{gs_scaling.rem} and Remark~\ref{scaling.rem} below, if $p=1+\frac4N$ and $u$ is a minimizer of $J^{1+\frac{4}{N},N}$, the Euler--Lagrange equation \eqref{euler} reads \begin{equation} \Delta u + \frac{c}{|x|^2} u -\frac{2}{N}\frac{H(u)}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2} u +|u|^{p-1}u=0, \end{equation} and any solution $u$ can be rescaled into a solution $Q$ of \eqref{sinls} by letting \[ u(x)=\lambda^{N/2}Q(\lambda x) \quad\text{with}\quad \lambda=\sqrt{\frac{2}{N}}\frac{\sqrt{H(u)}}{\Vert u\Vert_{L^2}}. \] The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: In the critical case, rescale any minimizer into a solution of the stationary equation.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Reduction via blow-up alternative
nodes.statement: Consider a local solution of \eqref{inls}, as given by Theorem~\ref{local.thm}. By the blow-up alternative, we need only show that, if $\Vert u_0\Vert_{L^2}<M_\text{gs}$, then $H(u(t))$ remains bounded.
nodes.statement_short: By the blow-up alternative it suffices to bound $H(u(t))$.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Express $H$ through the energy
nodes.statement: We control $H(u(t))$ using the energy. By definition of $E$, \[ H(u)=2E(u) + \frac{1}{1+\frac2N}\Vert{u}\Vert_{L^{2+\frac4N}}^{2+\frac4N}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $H(u)$ in terms of $E(u)$ and the $L^{2+4/N}$ norm.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Apply Gagliardo--Nirenberg
nodes.statement: Now, by Corollary~\ref{GN.cor}, \[ \|u\|_{L^{2+\frac4N}}^{2+\frac4N}\le \left(\frac{1+\frac2N}{M_\text{gs}^{\frac4N}}\right) H(u)\|u\|_{L^2}^{\frac4N} =(1+\textstyle\frac2N)\displaystyle\left(\frac{\|u\|_{L^2}}{M_\text{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(u). \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound the potential term by the sharp GN inequality.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Conclude the a priori bound
nodes.statement: Hence, by conservation of mass and energy, \begin{align*} H(u(t)) &\le 2E(u(t))+\left(\frac{\|u(t)\|_{L^2}}{M_\text{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(u(t))\\ &\phantom{\le}=2E(u_0)+\left(\frac{\|u_0\|_{L^2}}{M_\text{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(u(t)). \end{align*} It follows that \[ \left(1-\left(\frac{\|u_0\|_{L^2}}{M_\text{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}\right)H(u(t))\le 2 E(u_0), \] which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Conservation laws give a uniform bound on $H(u(t))$.
nodes.section: 2 Ground states and the sharp global existence criterion

nodes.name: Derivatives of $u_T$
nodes.statement: Straightforward calculations give \[ \partial_t u_T(t,x) = \frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}} \left[ \frac{N}{2}(T-t)u -i\frac{|x|^2}{4}u +\partial_t u +x\cdot\nabla u \right]\! \left(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\right) \] and \[ \Delta u_T(t,x) = \frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}} \left[ -\frac{|x|^2}{4}u -i\frac{N}{2}(T-t)u -ix\cdot\nabla u +\Delta u\right]\! \left(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\right) \] for the derivatives.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\partial_t u_T$ and $\Delta u_T$.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of minimal mass blow up solutions

nodes.name: Nonlinear and potential terms
nodes.statement: For the nonlinear term we find \[ |u_T|^{\frac{4}{N}}u_T(t,x)= \frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}}|u|^{\frac{4}{N}}u\Big(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\Big), \] and for the potential term \[ c|x|^{-2}u_T(t,x)= c\Big|\frac{x}{T-t}\Big|^{-2}\frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}}u\Big(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\Big). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute the nonlinear and inverse-square terms for $u_T$.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of minimal mass blow up solutions

nodes.name: Combine terms
nodes.statement: It then follows from \eqref{inls} that \[ \begin{split} i\partial u_T(t,x)+&\Delta u_T(t,x)+c|x|^{-2}u_T(t,x)+|u_T|^{4/N}u_T(t,x) \\ &=\frac{e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}}}{(T-t)^{N/2+2}}[i\partial_tu+\Delta u+c|x|^{-2}u +|u|^{4/N}u]\Big(\frac{1}{T-t},\frac{x}{T-t}\Big)=0, \end{split} \] which proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the terms and use the equation for $u$.
nodes.section: 3 Construction of minimal mass blow up solutions

nodes.name: $v$ and $|v|$ are minimizers
nodes.statement: It follows directly from \eqref{valueofmin} and \eqref{varchar} that $v$ is a minimizer of $J^{1+\frac4N,N}$. Since $J^{1+\frac4N,N}(|v|)\le J^{1+\frac4N,N}(v)$, $|v|$ is also a minimizer.
nodes.statement_short: By (2.5) and (4.1), $v$ and $|v|$ minimize $J$.

nodes.name: Positive minimizers are radial
nodes.statement: Furthermore, any positive minimizer is radial. Indeed, suppose $v_0$ is a positive minimizer that is not radial, and let $v_0^*$ be its Schwarz symmetrization. Then, in view of \cite[Theorem~3.4]{Lieb}, we have that \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{|v_0^*|^{2}}{|x|^2} dx > \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{|v_0|^{2}}{|x|^2} dx. \] Since, on the other hand, \[ \Vert \nabla v_0^*\Vert_{L^2}\le \Vert \nabla v_0\Vert_{L^2} \quad\text{and}\quad \Vert v_0^*\Vert_{L^2}\le\Vert v_0\Vert_{L^2}, \] we get $J^{1+\frac4N,N}(v_0^*)<J^{1+\frac4N,N}(v_0)$, a contradiction. We deduce that $|v|$ is radial.
nodes.statement_short: Strict Schwarz-symmetrization inequality for the Hardy term shows positive minimizers are radial.

nodes.name: $|v|$ is a rescaled ground state
nodes.statement: Now, $|v|$ satisfies the Euler--Lagrange equation \eqref{euler2} and we know there exists $Q\in\mathcal{G}$ such that \[ |v(x)|=\lambda_0^{N/2}Q(\lambda_0 x), \quad \text{where} \quad \lambda_0 =\Big(\frac{2}{N}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{H(|v|)^\frac{1}{2}}{\|v\|_{L^2}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Via (2.4), $|v|$ is a rescaled ground state.

nodes.name: Reduce to constant phase
nodes.statement: The proof will be complete if we show that $w(x)=v(x)/|v(x)|$ is constant on $\mathbb{R}^N$, for this implies that there exists $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $w(x)=e^{i\gamma_0}$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show the phase $w=v/|v|$ is constant.

nodes.name: Gradient decomposition
nodes.statement:
Differentiating $|w|^2=1$ yields $e(\overline{w}
abla w)\equiv 0$, thus \[ |
abla v|^2=|
abla(|v|)|^2+|v|^2|
abla w|^2+2|v|
abla(|v|)\cdot e(\overline{w}
abla w) \] and \[ \|
abla v\|_{L^2}^2=\|
abla (|v|)\|_{L^2}^2+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |v|^2|
abla w|^2dx. \]
nodes.statement_short: Split $\|\nabla v\|^2$ into modulus and phase parts.

nodes.name: Phase is constant
nodes.statement: Together with Hardy's inequality, this implies that, if $|\nabla w|\neq 0$ then $J^{1+\frac4N,N}(|v|)< J^{1+\frac4N,N}(v)$, which is a contradiction. Hence, $w$ is constant, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: A nonconstant phase would strictly increase $J$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Proof outline
nodes.statement: The behavior of the sequence $\{v_n\}$ is constrained by the concentration-compactness lemma. Our proof proceeds in several steps: by ruling out (V) and (D), we will first show that property (C) holds in Lemma~\ref{conc-comp.lemma}. We will then prove the localization of the subsequence $\{v_{n_k}\}$, {\em i.e.}~that the sequence of translations ${y_k}$ is bounded in $\mathbb{R}^N$. This step is the most delicate one due to the inverse-square potential, and will be handled by a subtle combination of Hardy's inequality and the Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality \eqref{GN}. Once this localization property is established, the result will follow from Proposition~\ref{charact.prop}.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: rule out (V) and (D), localize translations, apply Proposition 3.

nodes.name: Step 1: Compactness in $L^q$
nodes.statement: {\em Step~1: Compactness in $L^q(\mathbb{R}^N)$.} First suppose that (V) holds. Since $p+1\in (2,2^*)$ we get, \[ \limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty} E(v_{n_k})=\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}\Big\{\frac{1}{2}H(v_{n_k})-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx\Big\}=\frac{1}{2}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})>0, \] which contradicts our assumptions. Suppose now that (D) holds. Then from properties (5) and (6) it follows that \[ \begin{split} \limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}\{E(w_k)+E(z_k)\}&\le\frac{1}{2}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}) -\frac{1}{p+1}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|dx \\ &\le\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty} E(v_{n_k})\le 0. \end{split} \] Property (D)(4) of Lemma (\ref{conc-comp.lemma}) and inequality \eqref{posE} imply that $E(w_k), E(z_k)\ge 0$ for $k$ large enough, thus \[ E(w_k)\rightarrow 0 \quad \text{and} \quad E(z_k)\rightarrow 0. \] Using again property (4) and inequality \eqref{posE}, we get that \[ H(w_k)\rightarrow 0 \quad\text{and}\quad H(z_k)\rightarrow 0. \] Hence, \[ \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx =\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|z_k|^{p+1}dx\right)=0, \] leading again to the contradiction that $\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})>0$. Consequently, by Lemma~\ref{conc-comp.lemma}, there exists $v\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and a sequence of translations $\{y_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset \mathbb{R}^N$ such that \begin{equation} \widetilde{v}_{n_k} \rightarrow v \quad \text{in} \quad L^q(\mathbb{R}^N), \quad \forall q\in[2,2^*), \end{equation} where we let \[ \widetilde{v}_{n_k}(x):=v_{n_k}(x-y_k). \] In particular, the sequence $\{\widetilde{v}_{n_k}\}$ is compact in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and, in view of \eqref{a}, $\|v\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$. We shall also suppose, without loss of generality, that $\widetilde{v}_{n_k}\rightharpoonup v$ weakly in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rule out vanishing and dichotomy, so compactness up to translation holds.

nodes.name: Vanishing excluded
nodes.statement: {\em Step~1: Compactness in $L^q(\mathbb{R}^N)$.} First suppose that (V) holds. Since $p+1\in (2,2^*)$ we get, \[ \limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty} E(v_{n_k})=\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}\Big\{\frac{1}{2}H(v_{n_k})-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx\Big\}=\frac{1}{2}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})>0, \] which contradicts our assumptions.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing would force positive limiting energy.

nodes.name: Dichotomy excluded
nodes.statement: Suppose now that (D) holds. Then from properties (5) and (6) it follows that \[ \begin{split} \limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}\{E(w_k)+E(z_k)\}&\le\frac{1}{2}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}) -\frac{1}{p+1}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|dx \\ &\le\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty} E(v_{n_k})\le 0. \end{split} \] Property (D)(4) of Lemma (\ref{conc-comp.lemma}) and inequality \eqref{posE} imply that $E(w_k), E(z_k)\ge 0$ for $k$ large enough, thus \[ E(w_k)\rightarrow 0 \quad \text{and} \quad E(z_k)\rightarrow 0. \] Using again property (4) and inequality \eqref{posE}, we get that \[ H(w_k)\rightarrow 0 \quad\text{and}\quad H(z_k)\rightarrow 0. \] Hence, \[ \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx =\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|z_k|^{p+1}dx\right)=0, \] leading again to the contradiction that $\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Dichotomy forces $H(w_k),H(z_k)\to0$ via (1.8), again a contradiction.

nodes.name: Compactness up to translation
nodes.statement: Consequently, by Lemma~\ref{conc-comp.lemma}, there exists $v\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and a sequence of translations $\{y_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset \mathbb{R}^N$ such that \begin{equation} \widetilde{v}_{n_k} \rightarrow v \quad \text{in} \quad L^q(\mathbb{R}^N), \quad \forall q\in[2,2^*), \end{equation} where we let \[ \widetilde{v}_{n_k}(x):=v_{n_k}(x-y_k). \] In particular, the sequence $\{\widetilde{v}_{n_k}\}$ is compact in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and, in view of \eqref{a}, $\|v\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$. We shall also suppose, without loss of generality, that $\widetilde{v}_{n_k}\rightharpoonup v$ weakly in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence case (C): translates converge in $L^q$ to $v$ with mass $M_{gs}$.

nodes.name: Step 2: Localization
nodes.statement:
{\em Step~2: Localization.} We now prove by contradiction that the sequence of translations $\{y_k\}$ is bounded in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Let us assume that there exists a subsequence, denoted again by $\{y_k\}$, such that $|y_k|ightarrow\infty$ as $kightarrow\infty$. We will prove that, in this case, $\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})>0$, which contradicts \eqref{a}. We start by showing that  egin{equation} \lim_{k	o\infty} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}  rac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx = 0. \end{equation} To prove \eqref{zerolimit}, we split the integral as \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}  rac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx = \underbrace{\int_{|x|<R} rac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx}_{\mathrm{I}_k} +\underbrace{\int_{|x|\ge R} rac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx}_{\mathrm{II}_k}, \] for some $R>0$. Then define \[ u_k(x)=\varphi(|x|) v_{n_k}(x) \quad\text{and}\quad w_k(x)=(1-\varphi(|x|))v_{n_k}(x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Split $v_{n_k}=u_k+w_k$ with a radial cut-off.

nodes.name: Gradient bounds for pieces
nodes.statement:
We clearly have $|u_k|,|w_k|\le|v_{n_k}|$, and $\{u_k\},\{w_k\}\subset H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ with \[ |
abla u_k|^2 \le 2\left((\varphi')^2|v_{n_k}|^2+\varphi^2|
abla v_{n_k}|^2ight) \le 2\left(a^{-2}|v_{n_k}|^2+|
abla v_{n_k}|^2ight) \] and \[ |
abla w_k|^2 \le 2\left((\varphi')^2|v_{n_k}|^2+(1-\varphi)^2|
abla v_{n_k}|^2ight) \le 2\left(a^{-2}|v_{n_k}|^2+|
abla v_{n_k}|^2ight). \]
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise gradient bounds for $u_k,w_k$.

nodes.name: Hardy gives $H(u_k)$ bound
nodes.statement: Furthermore, \begin{equation*} \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{|u_k|^2}{|x|^2}dx\ge \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{|x|<R}\frac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx\ge\delta, \end{equation*} and \eqref{hardy} yields \begin{equation} \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(u_k)=\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty} \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |\nabla u_k|^2dx-c\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{|u_k|^2}{|x|^2}dx\right) \ge (c_*-c)\delta>0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Hardy's inequality gives $\liminf H(u_k)\ge(c_*-c)\delta$.

nodes.name: Decompose $H(v_{n_k})$
nodes.statement:
Using the sequences $\{u_k\},\{w_k\}$, we can now rewrite $H(v_{n_k})$ as  egin{align*} H(v_{n_k}) &=H(u_k)+H(w_k) \ &\phantom{=}+\int_{R<|x|<R+a} \Big[|
abla v_{n_k}|^2-|
abla u_k|^2-|
abla w_k|^2 - rac{c}{|x|^2}\left(|v_{n_k}|^2-|u_k|^2-|w_k|^2ight)\Big]dx. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $H(v_{n_k})=H(u_k)+H(w_k)+$ annulus error.

nodes.name: Goal: annulus error small
nodes.statement:
We will show that there exist $R>0$ as large as we want and $a>0$ such that, up to a further subsequence,  egin{equation} \limsup_{k	o\infty}\left|\int_{R<|x|<R+a} \Big[|
abla v_{n_k}|^2-|
abla u_k|^2-|
abla w_k|^2 - rac{c}{|x|^2}\left(|v_{n_k}|^2-|u_k|^2-|w_k|^2ight)\Big]dxight|\le rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{2}. \end{equation} Using \eqref{crucial}, this will imply  egin{equation} \liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}) \ge\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(w_k)+ rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{2}>\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(w_k), \end{equation} which will lead to the desired contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to make the annulus error at most $(c_*-c)\delta/2$, yielding (4.8).

nodes.name: Bound the annulus error
nodes.statement:
To prove \eqref{est0}, we use the above properties of $u_k$ and $w_k$ to observe that  egin{multline} \left|\int_{R<|x|<R+a}\Big[|
abla v_{n_k}|^2-|
abla u_k|^2-|
abla w_k|^2 - rac{c}{|x|^2}\left(|v_{n_k}|^2-|u_k|^2-|w_k|^2ight)\Big]dxight| \ \le 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|
abla v_{n_k}|^2dx+4a^{-2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx + rac{3c}{R^2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx. \end{multline} First, by choosing $R>0$ sufficiently large, we will have  egin{equation}  rac{3c}{R^2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx \le  rac{3c}{R^2} \|v_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 \le  rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad	ext{for all} \ k\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation} The second term in the right-hand side of \eqref{est} is handled using Step 1 with $|y_k|	o\infty$: for any fixed $R,a>0$, we have that  egin{equation} \lim_{k	o\infty} \int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx=0. \end{equation} As for the first term, we claim that we can choose $R>0$ as large as we want and $a>0$ such that, up to a subsequence,  egin{equation} 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|
abla v_{n_k}|^2dx\le  rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad	ext{for all} \ k\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation} Estimates \eqref{term3}--\eqref{term1} prove \eqref{est0}, and hence \eqref{e1}. If the above claim is not true, then using a diagonal argument we can construct a subsequence $\{v_{n_{k_l}}\}$, and a sequence of pairwise disjoint annuli \[ A_j=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N : R_j<|x|<R_j+a_j\} \quad	ext{with}\quad R_{j+1}>R_j+a_j, \] such that, for all $j\in\{1,\dots,l\}$, \[ \int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx\ge  ar \delta:=  rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{20}>0 \quad	ext{for all} \ n_{k_l}\in\mathbb{N}. \] But then \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge \sum_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge \sum_{j=1}^l\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge l ar\delta, \] and it follows that \[ \lim_{l	o\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx=+\infty. \] In view of \eqref{hardy2} this contradicts \eqref{a}, and completes the proof of \eqref{e1}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the annulus error by three terms and control each.

nodes.name: Three-term bound
nodes.statement:
To prove \eqref{est0}, we use the above properties of $u_k$ and $w_k$ to observe that  egin{multline} \left|\int_{R<|x|<R+a}\Big[|
abla v_{n_k}|^2-|
abla u_k|^2-|
abla w_k|^2 - rac{c}{|x|^2}\left(|v_{n_k}|^2-|u_k|^2-|w_k|^2ight)\Big]dxight| \ \le 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|
abla v_{n_k}|^2dx+4a^{-2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx + rac{3c}{R^2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx. \end{multline}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the error by gradient, mass and potential terms on the annulus.

nodes.name: Potential term
nodes.statement: First, by choosing $R>0$ sufficiently large, we will have \begin{equation} \frac{3c}{R^2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx \le \frac{3c}{R^2} \|v_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 \le \frac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad\text{for all} \ k\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Large $R$ makes the potential term small.

nodes.name: Mass term
nodes.statement: The second term in the right-hand side of \eqref{est} is handled using Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$: for any fixed $R,a>0$, we have that \begin{equation} \lim_{k\to\infty} \int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$ kills the annular mass.

nodes.name: Gradient term claim
nodes.statement: As for the first term, we claim that we can choose $R>0$ as large as we want and $a>0$ such that, up to a subsequence, \begin{equation} 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|\nabla v_{n_k}|^2dx\le \frac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad\text{for all} \ k\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the annular gradient term can be made small.

nodes.name: Combine estimates
nodes.statement: Estimates \eqref{term3}--\eqref{term1} prove \eqref{est0}, and hence \eqref{e1}.
nodes.statement_short: The three estimates give (4.7) and (4.8).

nodes.name: Proof of the claim
nodes.statement:
If the above claim is not true, then using a diagonal argument we can construct a subsequence $\{v_{n_{k_l}}\}$, and a sequence of pairwise disjoint annuli \[ A_j=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N : R_j<|x|<R_j+a_j\} \quad	ext{with}\quad R_{j+1}>R_j+a_j, \] such that, for all $j\in\{1,\dots,l\}$, \[ \int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx\ge  ar \delta:=  rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{20}>0 \quad	ext{for all} \ n_{k_l}\in\mathbb{N}. \] But then \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge \sum_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge \sum_{j=1}^l\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge l ar\delta, \] and it follows that \[ \lim_{l	o\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx=+\infty. \] In view of \eqref{hardy2} this contradicts \eqref{a}, and completes the proof of \eqref{e1}.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise disjoint annuli carry gradient mass, so $\|\nabla v\|_2\to\infty$, contradicting (4.2).

nodes.name: Energy inequality for $w_k$
nodes.statement: We will now combine \eqref{e1} with the Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality \eqref{GN} and the assumption on the energy in \eqref{a} to reach a contradiction. Using Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$, we have that $u_k\to0$ in $L^{p+1}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Hence, by \eqref{a}, \begin{align*} \limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})\le\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx =\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx, \end{align*} and so, by \eqref{e1}, \begin{align} \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k)<\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Since $u_k\to0$ in $L^{p+1}$, (4.2) and (4.8) give (4.13).

nodes.name: Mass of $w_k$
nodes.statement: Using again Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$, we also have that $u_k\to0$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$, which implies \[ M_\mathrm{gs}=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\|v_{n_k}\|_{L^2} =\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\|w_k\|_{L^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $u_k\to0$ in $L^2$, so $\|w_k\|_2\to M_{gs}$.

nodes.name: Gagliardo--Nirenberg contradiction
nodes.statement: Therefore, \eqref{GN} applied to $w_k$ yields \[ \frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx \le\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{\|w_k\|_{L^2}}{M_\mathrm{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(w_k) = \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k), \] which, together with \eqref{e4}, leads to the contradiction \[ \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k)<\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k). \]
nodes.statement_short: GN applied to $w_k$ contradicts (4.13).

nodes.name: Conclude (4.5)
nodes.statement: This shows that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathrm{I}_k=0$ and completes the proof of \eqref{zerolimit}.
nodes.statement_short: So the inner part vanishes, proving (4.5).

nodes.name: Positive energy contradiction
nodes.statement:
We now have  egin{align*} \liminf_{k	o\infty} E(v_{n_k}) &=\liminf_{k	o\infty}  rac12 \|
abla v_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 -\lim_{k	o\infty}  rac{1}{p+1} \| v_{n_k}\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\ &=\liminf_{k	o\infty}  rac12 \|
abla \widetilde{v}_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 -\lim_{k	o\infty}  rac{1}{p+1} \| \widetilde{v}_{n_k}\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\ &\ge  rac12 \|
abla v\|_{L^2}^2 -  rac{1}{p+1} \|v\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}>E(v)\ge 0, \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from \eqref{posE} with $\|v\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$. This contradicts \eqref{a} and shows that the sequence $\{y_k\}$ must indeed be bounded in $\mathbb{R}^N$.
nodes.statement_short: With the Hardy term gone, lower semicontinuity and (1.8) give positive energy, contradicting (4.2).

nodes.name: Step 3: Conclusion
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3: Conclusion.} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $y_k\to y^*\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Then \[ v_{n_k}\to v^*=v(\cdot+y^*) \quad \text{in} \quad L^q(\mathbb{R}^N), \quad \forall q\in[2,2^*), \] and $v_{n_k}\rightharpoonup v^*$ weakly in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Since the Hardy functional $H$ is weakly lower semi-continuous \cite{montefusco}, and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, it now follows by \eqref{posE} that \[ \begin{split} 0\le E(v^*)=\frac{1}{2}H(v^*)-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx &\le \frac{1}{2}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx\\ &\phantom{\le}=\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})\le 0, \end{split} \] so in fact \begin{equation} E(v^*)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad H(v^*)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}). \end{equation} Since $\|v^*\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(v^*)=0$, Proposition \ref{charact.prop} yields $v^*=e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda_0>0$, and some $Q\in \mathcal{G}$. Finally, by \eqref{convergence} and \eqref{hardy2}, we also have that $\|v_{n_k}\|_{H^1}\rightarrow \|v^*\|_{H^1}$. Hence $\{v_{n_k}\}$ converges strongly to $v^*$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Strong $H^1$ convergence to a phase-shifted rescaled ground state.

nodes.name: Limit $v^*$
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3: Conclusion.} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $y_k\to y^*\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Then \[ v_{n_k}\to v^*=v(\cdot+y^*) \quad \text{in} \quad L^q(\mathbb{R}^N), \quad \forall q\in[2,2^*), \] and $v_{n_k}\rightharpoonup v^*$ weakly in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Translations converge, so $v_{n_k}\to v^*$ in $L^q$ and weakly in $H^1$.

nodes.name: Zero energy of the limit
nodes.statement: Since the Hardy functional $H$ is weakly lower semi-continuous \cite{montefusco}, and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, it now follows by \eqref{posE} that \[ \begin{split} 0\le E(v^*)=\frac{1}{2}H(v^*)-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx &\le \frac{1}{2}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx\\ &\phantom{\le}=\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})\le 0, \end{split} \] so in fact \begin{equation} E(v^*)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad H(v^*)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Weak lsc and (1.8) give $E(v^*)=0$ and convergence of $H$.

nodes.name: Identify the limit
nodes.statement: Since $\|v^*\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(v^*)=0$, Proposition \ref{charact.prop} yields $v^*=e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda_0>0$, and some $Q\in \mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3 identifies $v^*$ as a rescaled ground state.

nodes.name: Strong convergence
nodes.statement: Finally, by \eqref{convergence} and \eqref{hardy2}, we also have that $\|v_{n_k}\|_{H^1}\rightarrow \|v^*\|_{H^1}$. Hence $\{v_{n_k}\}$ converges strongly to $v^*$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Norm convergence upgrades weak to strong $H^1$ convergence.

nodes.name: Regularization
nodes.statement: By regularization we may assume that $u$ is smooth enough for the following calculation.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $u$ smooth by regularization.

nodes.statement:
Since $u$ satisfies (ef{inls}), we find \[  egin{split} \Gamma'(t)&=2e\int|x|^2 ar{u}\partial_tu=2e\int|x|^2 ar{u}i(\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u)\ &=-2\im\int|x|^2( ar{u}\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}|u|^2+|u|^{p+1})=-2\im\int|x|^2 ar{u}\Delta u. \end{split} \] Integrating by parts and using that $

nodes.statement_short: Differentiate $\Gamma$ and integrate by parts to get (4.15).

nodes.statement:
Using again integration by parts, we get \[  egin{split} \Gamma''(t)&=4\im\int\partial_t ar{u}(x\cdot
abla u)+ ar{u}(x\cdot
abla\partial_tu) =4\im\int\partial_tu[-x\cdot

abla\cdot x] =-8\im\int\partial_tu(x\cdot

nodes.statement_short: Differentiate again and integrate by parts.

nodes.name: First term via the equation
nodes.statement: We use (\ref{inls}) to compute the last two terms. We first find \begin{align} -4N\im\int\partial_tu\bar{u}&=-4N\re\int\bar{u}(\Delta u+\frac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u)\notag \\ &=4N\int{|\nabla u|^2}-4Nc\int\frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}-4N\int|u|^{p+1}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Split second term
nodes.statement:
Similarly, \[  egin{split} -8\im\int\partial_tu(x\cdot 
abla  ar{u})&= -8e\int(x\cdot

nodes.statement_short: Split the remaining term into $A+B+C$.

nodes.name: Compute $A$
nodes.statement:
Since $\partial_{x_k}(|\partial_{x_j}u|^2) = 2e(\partial_{x_j}u\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x_k} ar u)$ for $1\le j,k\le N$, we find  egin{align} A &= -8\sum_{j,k} e\int \partial_{x_j}^2u\, x_k\partial_{x_k} ar u = 8\sum_{j,k} e\int \partial_{x_j}u (\delta_{j,k}\partial_{x_k} ar u + x_k\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x_k} ar u) 
otag \ &= 8\sum_j \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 +4\sum_{j,k} \int x_k\partial_{x_k}(|\partial_{x_j}u|^2) 
otag \ &= 8\sum_j \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 -4\sum_{j,k} \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 = (8-4N)\int |

nodes.statement_short: Compute $A=(8-4N)\|\nabla u\|_2^2$.

nodes.name: Compute $C$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $C$ by integration by parts.

nodes.statement_short: Compute the potential term $B$.

nodes.name: Assemble
nodes.statement: Finally, putting together (\ref{viriala}), (\ref{virialpart3}), (\ref{virialc}) and (\ref{viriald}), we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Gamma''(t)&=8\int|\nabla u|^2-8c\int\frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}+\frac{4}{p+1}(N-Np)\int|u|^{p+1} \\ &=16E(u)+\frac{4}{p+1}(N-Np+4)\int|u|^{p+1}, \end{split} \] which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the terms to obtain (4.16).

nodes.name: Setting
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be a solution of \eqref{inls} such that $\|u\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $\lim_{t\uparrow T} H(u) =+\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $u$ be a minimal mass solution blowing up at $T$.

nodes.name: Step 1: Rescaled sequence converges
nodes.statement: {\em Step~1.} Let $\{t_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of times such that $t_n\uparrow T$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We set \[ u_n=u(t_n), \quad \lambda_n^2=H(u_n), \quad v_n(x)=\lambda_n^{-N/2}u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x). \] We note that $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, and $\|v_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ by the $L^2$ scaling. Furthermore, \[ \begin{split} H(v_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)=1. \end{split} \] On the other hand, by conservation of the energy, \[ \begin{split} E(v_n)&=\frac12\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)-\frac{1}{p+1}\lambda_n^{-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u_n(y)|^{p+1}dy\\ &=\lambda_n^{-2} E(u_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}E(u_0)\to 0 \quad \text{as} \ n\to\infty. \end{split} \] Hence, by Proposition \ref{compact.prop}, there exist $Q\in\mathcal{G}$, $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\lambda_0>0$ such that, up to a subsequence, \begin{equation} \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \|v_n-e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}\|_{H^1}=0, \end{equation} where $Q_{\lambda_0}(x)=\lambda_0^{N/2}Q(\lambda_0 x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale along $t_n\uparrow T$ and apply Proposition 4.

nodes.name: Rescaled sequence
nodes.statement: {\em Step~1.} Let $\{t_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of times such that $t_n\uparrow T$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We set \[ u_n=u(t_n), \quad \lambda_n^2=H(u_n), \quad v_n(x)=\lambda_n^{-N/2}u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $u_n$, $\lambda_n$ and the rescaled $v_n$.

nodes.name: Mass and $H$ of $v_n$
nodes.statement: We note that $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, and $\|v_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ by the $L^2$ scaling. Furthermore, \[ \begin{split} H(v_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)=1. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: $v_n$ has mass $M_{gs}$ and $H(v_n)=1$.

nodes.name: Energy of $v_n$ vanishes
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by conservation of the energy, \[ \begin{split} E(v_n)&=\frac12\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)-\frac{1}{p+1}\lambda_n^{-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u_n(y)|^{p+1}dy\\ &=\lambda_n^{-2} E(u_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}E(u_0)\to 0 \quad \text{as} \ n\to\infty. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: $E(v_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}E(u_0)\to0$.

nodes.name: Apply compactness
nodes.statement: Hence, by Proposition \ref{compact.prop}, there exist $Q\in\mathcal{G}$, $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\lambda_0>0$ such that, up to a subsequence, \begin{equation} \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \|v_n-e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}\|_{H^1}=0, \end{equation} where $Q_{\lambda_0}(x)=\lambda_0^{N/2}Q(\lambda_0 x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4 gives convergence to a rescaled ground state.

nodes.name: Step 2: Mass concentration
nodes.statement: {\em Step~2.} We now prove that $u_n$ concentrates all of its mass at $x=0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We show that, in the sense of distributions, \[ |u_n|^2\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\delta_0. \] Indeed, for any $\varphi\in C^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$, using the change of variables $y=\lambda_n^{-1}x$ we find that \[ \begin{split} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x)|^2\varphi(\lambda^{-1}_nx)\lambda_n^{-N}dx =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_n(x)|^2\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(|v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2)\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |Q(x)|^2\varphi(0)dx\\ &\phantom{\le} \ +\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|Q(x)|^2(\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0))dx. \end{split} \] Thus, we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy -M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0)\Big| &\le \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}||v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2|dx\\ &\phantom{\le} \ +\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|Q(x)|^2|\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0)|dx. \end{split} \] We conclude this step by noticing that $|v_n|^2$ converges strongly to $|Q|^2$ in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ from (\ref{b}), so the first integral vanishes as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Since $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ the second integral also converges to zero by the dominated convergence theorem. Hence, we obtain \begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $|u_n|^2\to M_{gs}^2\delta_0$ in distributions.

nodes.name: Concentration claim
nodes.statement: {\em Step~2.} We now prove that $u_n$ concentrates all of its mass at $x=0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We show that, in the sense of distributions, \[ |u_n|^2\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\delta_0. \]
nodes.statement_short: State the concentration claim.

nodes.name: Change of variables
nodes.statement: Indeed, for any $\varphi\in C^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$, using the change of variables $y=\lambda_n^{-1}x$ we find that \[ \begin{split} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x)|^2\varphi(\lambda^{-1}_nx)\lambda_n^{-N}dx =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_n(x)|^2\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(|v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2)\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |Q(x)|^2\varphi(0)dx\\ &\phantom{\le} \ +\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|Q(x)|^2(\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0))dx. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Change variables to express the integral through $v_n$ and $Q$.

nodes.name: Error bound
nodes.statement: Thus, we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy -M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0)\Big| &\le \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}||v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2|dx\\ &\phantom{\le} \ +\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|Q(x)|^2|\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0)|dx. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound the deviation from $M_{gs}^2\varphi(0)$ by two integrals.

nodes.name: Both integrals vanish
nodes.statement: We conclude this step by noticing that $|v_n|^2$ converges strongly to $|Q|^2$ in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ from (\ref{b}), so the first integral vanishes as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Since $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ the second integral also converges to zero by the dominated convergence theorem. Hence, we obtain \begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Strong convergence and dominated convergence give (4.24).

nodes.name: Step 3: Finite variance and its exact form
nodes.statement:
{\em Step~3.} We now show that $u(t)\in\Sigma$ for all $t\in[0,T)$. Let $\phi\in C^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ be a radial and non-negative function such that $\phi(x)=|x|^2$ for $|x|\le 1$. It is easy to see that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \[ |
abla \phi (x) |^2\le C\phi(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Indeed, since $\phi$ is radially symmetric we may choose $f\in C(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}_+) $, such that $\phi(|x|)=f(|x|)$. By Taylor's formula, for all $r\in\mathbb{R}$ and $h\in\mathbb{R}$ there exists $y\in[r,r+h]$, such that \[ 0\le f(r+h)=f(r)+f'(r)h+ rac{f''(y)}{2}h^2\le f(r)+f'(r)h+C'h^2, \] where $C'=1+\max_{r\in\mathbb{R}} rac{|f'(r)|}{2}>0$. Since the right-hand side is a positive quadratic polynomial, we must have that $|f'(r)|^2-4C'f(r)\le 0$, thus $|f'(r)|^2\le Cf(r)$, where $C=4C'>0$. For all $R>0$, we define $\phi_R(x)=R^2\phi(x/R)$, and for all $t\in[0,T)$, \[ \Gamma_R(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\phi_R(x)|u(t,x)|^2dx. \] A direct calculation, similar to the proof of Lemma~ef{virial.lemma}, yields that \[ \Gamma_R'(t)=2	ext{Re}\int\phi_R ar{u}\partial_tu =-2	ext{Im}\int\phi_R ar{u}(\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u) =2\int
abla\phi_R\cdot	ext{Im}( ar{u}
abla u). \] Since $\|u\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$, we can apply Lemma ef{banica.lem} and the inequality $|
abla\phi_R|^2\le C\phi_R$, to get \[ |\Gamma'_R(t)|\le 2\sqrt{2E(u)}\Big(\int|
abla\phi_R|^2|u|^2\Big)^{1/2} \le C\sqrt{E(u_0)}\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}. \] By integrating between a fixed $t\in[0,T)$ and $t_n$, we obtain, \[ |\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}-\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t_n)}|\le C|t-t_n|. \] Applying (ef{c}) in Step 2, we get \[ \Gamma_R(t_n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u_n(x)|^2\phi_R(x)dxightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\phi_R(0)=0. \] Thus, letting $n	o\infty$ in the last inequality, we obtain, for all $t\in [0,T)$ and all $R>0$, \[ \Gamma_R(t) \le C(T-t)^2. \] Since the right-hand side of the last expression is independent of $R$, letting $R	o\infty$ yields, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ u(t)\in\Sigma \quad	ext{and}\quad 0\le \Gamma(t) \le C(T-t)^2. \] From this estimate, we can extend by continuity $\Gamma(t)$ at $t=T$ by setting $\Gamma(T)=0$, from which we also obtain $\Gamma'(T)=0$. Moreover, since $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $u$ is a solution of~\eqref{inls}, we may apply Lemma~ef{virial.lemma}, and by (ef{virialthree}) we obtain $\Gamma''(t)=16E(u_0)$, which finally gives, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ \Gamma(t) = 8E(u_0)(T-t)^2. \] Letting $t=0$, we find, using identity (ef{virialone}) \[ \Gamma(0)=\int |x|^2|u_0|^2= 8E(u_0)T^2 \quad 	ext{and}\quad \Gamma'(0)= 4\int x\cdot\im(\overline{u_0}
abla u_0) = -16E(u_0)T. \]
nodes.statement_short: Show $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $\Gamma(t)=8E(u_0)(T-t)^2$.

nodes.name: Cut-off weight $\phi$
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3.} We now show that $u(t)\in\Sigma$ for all $t\in[0,T)$. Let $\phi\in C^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ be a radial and non-negative function such that $\phi(x)=|x|^2$ for $|x|\le 1$. It is easy to see that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \[ |\nabla \phi (x) |^2\le C\phi(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a weight $\phi$ with $|\nabla\phi|^2\le C\phi$.

nodes.name: Proof of $|\nabla\phi|^2\le C\phi$
nodes.statement: Indeed, since $\phi$ is radially symmetric we may choose $f\in C(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}_+) $, such that $\phi(|x|)=f(|x|)$. By Taylor's formula, for all $r\in\mathbb{R}$ and $h\in\mathbb{R}$ there exists $y\in[r,r+h]$, such that \[ 0\le f(r+h)=f(r)+f'(r)h+\frac{f''(y)}{2}h^2\le f(r)+f'(r)h+C'h^2, \] where $C'=1+\max_{r\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{|f'(r)|}{2}>0$. Since the right-hand side is a positive quadratic polynomial, we must have that $|f'(r)|^2-4C'f(r)\le 0$, thus $|f'(r)|^2\le Cf(r)$, where $C=4C'>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Taylor's formula and a discriminant argument.

nodes.name: Localized variance
nodes.statement: For all $R>0$, we define $\phi_R(x)=R^2\phi(x/R)$, and for all $t\in[0,T)$, \[ \Gamma_R(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\phi_R(x)|u(t,x)|^2dx. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Gamma_R$.

nodes.name: Derivative of $\Gamma_R$
nodes.statement: A direct calculation, similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{virial.lemma}, yields that \[ \Gamma_R'(t)=2\text{Re}\int\phi_R\bar{u}\partial_tu =-2\text{Im}\int\phi_R\bar{u}(\Delta u+\frac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u) =2\int\nabla\phi_R\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u}\nabla u). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\Gamma_R'$ as for the virial identity.

nodes.name: Apply Banica's inequality
nodes.statement: Since $\|u\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$, we can apply Lemma \ref{banica.lem} and the inequality $|\nabla\phi_R|^2\le C\phi_R$, to get \[ |\Gamma'_R(t)|\le 2\sqrt{2E(u)}\Big(\int|\nabla\phi_R|^2|u|^2\Big)^{1/2} \le C\sqrt{E(u_0)}\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4 gives $|\Gamma_R'|\le C\sqrt{\Gamma_R}$.

nodes.name: Integrate
nodes.statement: By integrating between a fixed $t\in[0,T)$ and $t_n$, we obtain, \[ |\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}-\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t_n)}|\le C|t-t_n|. \]
nodes.statement_short: Integrate to bound $\sqrt{\Gamma_R}$ differences.

nodes.name: Bound $\Gamma_R$
nodes.statement: Applying (\ref{c}) in Step 2, we get \[ \Gamma_R(t_n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u_n(x)|^2\phi_R(x)dx\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\phi_R(0)=0. \] Thus, letting $n\to\infty$ in the last inequality, we obtain, for all $t\in [0,T)$ and all $R>0$, \[ \Gamma_R(t) \le C(T-t)^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Concentration gives $\Gamma_R(t)\le C(T-t)^2$.

nodes.name: Finite variance
nodes.statement: Since the right-hand side of the last expression is independent of $R$, letting $R\to\infty$ yields, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ u(t)\in\Sigma \quad\text{and}\quad 0\le \Gamma(t) \le C(T-t)^2. \] From this estimate, we can extend by continuity $\Gamma(t)$ at $t=T$ by setting $\Gamma(T)=0$, from which we also obtain $\Gamma'(T)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Letting $R\to\infty$, $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $\Gamma(T)=\Gamma'(T)=0$.

nodes.name: Exact variance
nodes.statement: Moreover, since $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $u$ is a solution of~\eqref{inls}, we may apply Lemma~\ref{virial.lemma}, and by (\ref{virialthree}) we obtain $\Gamma''(t)=16E(u_0)$, which finally gives, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ \Gamma(t) = 8E(u_0)(T-t)^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Virial identity gives $\Gamma(t)=8E(u_0)(T-t)^2$.

nodes.name: Initial data identities
nodes.statement: Letting $t=0$, we find, using identity (\ref{virialone}) \[ \Gamma(0)=\int |x|^2|u_0|^2= 8E(u_0)T^2 \quad \text{and}\quad \Gamma'(0)= 4\int x\cdot\im(\overline{u_0}\nabla u_0) = -16E(u_0)T. \]
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate $\Gamma(0)$ and $\Gamma'(0)$.

nodes.name: Step 4: Identification
nodes.statement: {\em Step 4.} We apply identity \eqref{valeria} with $u_0$, $s=\frac{1}{2T}$, and $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}$ to get \[ \begin{split} E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})&=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}\int x\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u_0}\nabla u_0) +\frac{1}{8T^2}\int|x|^2|u_0|^2\\ &=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}(-4E(u_0))+\frac{1}{8T^2}(8E(u_0)T^2)=0. \end{split} \] Note that this calculation justifies, {\em a posteriori}, the application of~\eqref{valeria} with $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}\not\in C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Since $\|u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})=0$, we can deduce from Proposition \ref{charact.prop} that there exist $\lambda_1>0$, $\gamma_1\in\mathbb{R}$, and $\widetilde{Q}\in\mathcal{G}$ such that \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\gamma_1}e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\lambda_1^{N/2}\widetilde{Q}(\lambda_1x). \] Finally, we use the pseudo-conformal transformation. We define $\tilde\lambda_0=\lambda_1T>0$ and $\tilde\gamma_0=\gamma_1-\lambda_1^2T\in\mathbb{R}$, and write $u_0$ as \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\tilde\gamma_0}e^{i\frac{\tilde\lambda^2_0}{T}} e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0}{T}\Big)^{N/2}\widetilde{Q}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0x}{T}\Big). \] Thus, $u_0=S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(0)$, where $S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}$ is defined by (\ref{S2.def}). By invoking uniqueness of the solution of (\ref{inls}), we find that $u(t)=S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(t)$ for all $t\in[0,T)$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Phase-modulated initial datum has zero energy; identify $u$ with $S_{Q,T,\lambda_0,\gamma_0}$.

nodes.name: Zero energy after modulation
nodes.statement: {\em Step 4.} We apply identity \eqref{valeria} with $u_0$, $s=\frac{1}{2T}$, and $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}$ to get \[ \begin{split} E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})&=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}\int x\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u_0}\nabla u_0) +\frac{1}{8T^2}\int|x|^2|u_0|^2\\ &=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}(-4E(u_0))+\frac{1}{8T^2}(8E(u_0)T^2)=0. \end{split} \] Note that this calculation justifies, {\em a posteriori}, the application of~\eqref{valeria} with $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}\not\in C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Identity (4.22) shows $E(u_0e^{i|x|^2/4T})=0$.

nodes.name: Characterize $u_0$
nodes.statement: Since $\|u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})=0$, we can deduce from Proposition \ref{charact.prop} that there exist $\lambda_1>0$, $\gamma_1\in\mathbb{R}$, and $\widetilde{Q}\in\mathcal{G}$ such that \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\gamma_1}e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\lambda_1^{N/2}\widetilde{Q}(\lambda_1x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3 identifies the modulated datum as a ground state.

nodes.name: Rewrite $u_0$
nodes.statement: Finally, we use the pseudo-conformal transformation. We define $\tilde\lambda_0=\lambda_1T>0$ and $\tilde\gamma_0=\gamma_1-\lambda_1^2T\in\mathbb{R}$, and write $u_0$ as \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\tilde\gamma_0}e^{i\frac{\tilde\lambda^2_0}{T}} e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0}{T}\Big)^{N/2}\widetilde{Q}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0x}{T}\Big). \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $u_0$ as $S_{\tilde Q,T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(0)$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: Thus, $u_0=S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(0)$, where $S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}$ is defined by (\ref{S2.def}). By invoking uniqueness of the solution of (\ref{inls}), we find that $u(t)=S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(t)$ for all $t\in[0,T)$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of solutions gives $u=S$.
